body.objective: Students will be able to shape phrases with dynamics.
body.iCan: I can shape phrases with dynamics.
successCriteria: I can identify phrases and their high points
I can shape phrases with dynamics and breathing
I can follow concert etiquette and show stage presence
body.hook: Play a melody with every note at the same volume and it sounds like a ringtone. Shape it, growing toward the high point and relaxing at the end, and it sounds like someone speaking. That shaping is called phrasing.

vocabulary.definition: A musical sentence, often four or eight bars long.
Levels of loud and soft, such as p, mf and f.
A comma-like sign showing where to breathe.
How a performer looks and behaves on stage.
Expected behaviour for performers and audiences at a concert.

study.title: Musical Sentences
study.question: How do musicians shape phrases and present a concert?
study.passage:
Part 1, Speak it (5 minutes): Read this sentence flat, then with natural expression: "I can't believe we actually won the championship." Where did your voice rise? Music works the same way.
Part 2, Find the phrase (10 minutes): In your concert piece, mark phrases with a bracket over each four- or eight-bar section. Circle the high point (often the highest or longest note, or where harmony is most tense).
Part 3, Shape it (15 minutes): Plan the dynamics: grow toward the high point and relax after it, even if the music only says "mf." Mark breath marks at phrase ends, never in the middle of a phrase. Play with a three-level plan: start, peak, end.
Part 4, Concert etiquette (10 minutes): Performers: walk on and off confidently; instruments up together on the conductor's signal; no talking or fidgeting; stay still at the end until the conductor lowers the arms; bow together. Audience: enter and leave between pieces; applaud at the end of a piece, not between movements; phones off.
Part 5, Run (10 minutes): Perform one piece as if it were the concert, from walk-on to bow.

examples.title: High point
examples.problem: Where is the high point of a phrase usually?
steps: Look for highest note or tension
examples.answer: Often near the middle to end of the phrase, on the highest or longest note

examples.title: Breath
examples.problem: Where should you breathe in an 8-bar phrase?
examples.answer: At the end of the phrase, not in the middle
examples.explore: What if you can't make it?

examples.title: Etiquette
examples.problem: When should the audience clap during a symphony?
examples.answer: At the end of the whole work, not between movements

examples.title: Stage presence
examples.problem: What should you do after the last note?
examples.answer: Hold your position until the conductor lowers the arms, then relax

practice.a: A musical sentence, often four or eight bars.
A sign showing where to breathe.
How a performer looks and behaves on stage.

practice.q: Why shape a phrase toward a high point?
practice.a: To make the music expressive, like speech.

practice.q: Name two rules of concert etiquette for performers.
practice.a: No talking, stay still at the end, instruments up together, bow together.
At the end of a complete piece.

practice.q: Order these from softest to loudest: f, p, mf, pp.
Why can a phrase have dynamics not written in the score?
practice.a: Musicians shape phrases within the written level for expression.

practice.q: How can a performer show stage presence before playing?
practice.a: Walk on confidently, sit or stand tall, focus on the conductor.

practice.q: What happens if players breathe in different places?
practice.a: The phrase is broken and the sound becomes uneven.

practice.q: How does phrasing make music sound like speech?
practice.a: Rising and relaxing volume mirror natural speech patterns.

misconceptions: Playing every note at the same volume
Breathing whenever you run out of air in the middle of a phrase
Thinking stage presence doesn't affect the music
exitTicket: Mark the high point of one phrase in your music.

items.q: Define phrase.
items.answer: A musical sentence, often four or eight bars.

items.q: What is a breath mark?
items.answer: A sign showing where to breathe.

items.q: Explain how to shape a phrase with dynamics.
items.answer: Grow toward the high point and relax after it.

items.q: List three concert etiquette rules for performers.
items.answer: No talking, instruments up together, stillness at the end, bow together.

items.q: Why breathe at phrase ends?
items.answer: To keep musical sentences unbroken.

items.q: Order pp, ff, mp, f from softest to loudest.
items.answer: pp, mp, f, ff.

items.q: Explain how phrasing is like speaking.
items.answer: Both rise and fall naturally to express meaning.

items.q: Describe how stage presence affects an audience's experience.
items.answer: Confident, focused performers draw the audience in and make the music more convincing.
